title: Super Pow
description: Brute force to optimized: an infeasible direct loop versus processing the huge exponent digit by digit, then a reusable fast-power helper for each step.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Problem Summary: Given a and a huge exponent b, given as an array of digits since it is too large for a normal integer, compute a raised to the power b, modulo 1337.

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given a positive number a and a huge positive number b (given as an array of its digits, since b can be far too large to fit in any normal integer type), compute a raised to the power b, modulo 1337.

blocks.title: Analogy: Reading a Number Too Long for the Page
blocks.text: Picture the exponent b written on a scroll so long it can never be unrolled and read all at once, only one digit visible at a time. Building the final answer means processing the scroll one digit at a time, folding each new digit into a running result, without ever needing to see or hold the entire huge number at once.

blocks.caption: Fold each digit of the exponent into a running, always-small result

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: a = 2, b = [3]

blocks.content: {"headers":["a","b (digits)","Result","Why"],"rows":[["2","[3]","8","The single digit 3 represents the exponent 3 directly, giving 2 cubed."]]}

blocks.text: This is simply 2 cubed, which is 8, already less than 1337 so no reduction is needed.
Example: a = 2, b = [1, 0]

blocks.content: {"headers":["a","b (digits)","Result","Why"],"rows":[["2","[1, 0]","1024","The digits 1 then 0 represent the two-digit exponent 10, giving 2 to the 10th power."]]}

blocks.text: The digits [1, 0] represent the number 10, so this is 2 to the power 10, which is 1024, still less than 1337.
1 raised to any power is always 1, regardless of how large the exponent is.
5. How Should We Think?
Before writing any code, it helps to reason about why b is given as an array of digits in the first place.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The exponent b can have up to 2000 digits, far too many to ever fit into or be reconstructed as a normal integer, and far too large to ever loop that many times directly.

Observation 2: Any multi-digit number can be built up one digit at a time: reading digits left to right, each new digit means take everything read so far, shift it one decimal place, then add this digit.

Observation 3: That same shift-then-add idea applies to exponents too, through the identity a to the power (10 times x plus d) equals (a to the power x) raised to the 10th power, times a to the power d, letting the huge exponent be processed one digit at a time without ever forming it as a whole number.

Observation 4: Taking everything modulo 1337 after every single multiplication keeps every intermediate value small and safe, regardless of how many digits b has or how large a itself is.
That reasoning alone already reveals the entire approach: never reconstruct b, fold its digits in one at a time using the tenth-power identity.
6. Brute Force Solution

The most literal approach is to try reading all of b's digits back into a single number, then multiply a into a running result that many times, taking the remainder modulo 1337 after every multiplication to keep the numbers small.
Step by step algorithm

items: Combine every digit in b back into a single number.
Start a running result at 1.
Multiply the result by a, and immediately take the result modulo 1337, repeating this once for every unit of b.
Return the final result.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: this only works for illustration, real inputs make it impossible

codes.python:
def super_pow(a, b):
    # WARNING: only works for illustration when b is small; the real
    # constraint gives b as up to 2000 digits, far too large to ever loop over
    b_value = int(''.join(map(str, b)))  # this line alone can fail for huge b
    result = 1
    for _ in range(b_value):
        result = (result * a) % 1337        # multiply and immediately reduce mod 1337
    return result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    a = 2
    b = [1, 0]
    print(super_pow(a, b))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The comment warning at the top of the function exists specifically because this code is included for illustration and contrast, not as a viable solution, reconstructing b_value alone can already overflow or take unbounded time for the real constraint.

The modulo reduction happens immediately after every single multiplication, inside the loop, rather than once at the very end, since waiting until the end would let result grow to an astronomically large, unrepresentable size long before the loop finishes.

This version is structured to mirror the direct mathematical definition, multiply a into the result once per unit of the exponent, precisely so its complete impracticality for a 2000-digit b is obvious and motivates the digit by digit approach that follows.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
For a small b, this approach is correct, since repeated multiplication with a modulo reduction after every step is a valid way to compute a power modulo 1337.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(b), one multiplication per unit of the exponent.
Space: O(1) beyond reconstructing b itself.

Limitation: this approach is not merely slow, it is genuinely impossible to run for the real constraint. b can be given as up to 2000 digits, a number so large that looping that many times could never finish, and simply reconstructing b as a single integer would overflow long before the loop even starts.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why looping b_value times fails, beyond just being slow: b_value itself cannot even be safely reconstructed as a single integer once b has more than a handful of digits.

What information is actually available: b's individual digits, one at a time, exactly how the problem chooses to represent it.

Is there a way to fold in one digit at a time, mathematically: yes, the identity a to the power (10 times x plus d) equals (a to the power x) raised to the 10th power, times a to the power d, expresses exactly that.

What does applying this identity require at each step: raising the current running result to the 10th power, then multiplying in a raised to the newly seen digit, both taken modulo 1337.

The core idea: walk b's digits left to right, and at each digit, raise the running result to the 10th power and multiply in a raised to that digit, both reduced modulo 1337.

The key identity is that a to the power (10 times x plus d) equals (a to the power x) raised to the 10th power, multiplied by a to the power d. This means the exponent can be built up one digit at a time, from most significant to least significant, without ever forming the full huge number b.
At every step, take the current running result, raise it to the 10th power (shifting the existing progress one decimal place), then multiply in a raised to the power of the newly seen digit.
9. Optimized Solution
Walk through the digits of b from left to right. At each digit, raise the running result to the 10th power modulo 1337, then multiply in a raised to that digit's value modulo 1337.
Dry run for a = 2, b = [1, 0]

blocks.content: {"headers":["Digit","result raised to the 10th","a raised to this digit","New result","Why"],"rows":[["1","1 to the 10th = 1","2 to the 1st = 2","1 times 2 = 2","The running result starts at 1, so raising it to the 10th stays 1; multiplying in a to this first digit folds in the digit itself."],["0","2 to the 10th = 1024","2 to the 0th = 1","1024 times 1 = 1024","Raising the previous result to the 10th shifts it one decimal place, and a digit of 0 contributes nothing further."]]}

blocks.text: The final result is 1024, exactly 2 to the power 10, confirming the digit by digit approach matches direct computation.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: fold in one digit of b at a time using the tenth-power identity

codes.python:
def super_pow(a, b):
    a %= 1337                       # reduce a first so it never grows large
    result = 1
    for digit in b:                   # walk through b's digits, most significant first
        power_result = 1
        for _ in range(10):
            power_result = (power_result * result) % 1337  # raise the running result to the 10th power
        digit_power = 1
        for _ in range(digit):
            digit_power = (digit_power * a) % 1337            # raise a to this digit's power
        result = (power_result * digit_power) % 1337           # combine both pieces for this digit
    return result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    a = 2
    b = [1, 0]
    print(super_pow(a, b))

blocks.text: Why This Works

This works because of the identity a to the power (10 times x plus d) equals (a to the power x raised to the 10th power) times (a to the power d): reading b's digits left to right, after processing some prefix of digits representing value x, seeing one more digit d extends the number being represented to exactly 10 times x plus d, and the identity says the corresponding power of a can be updated by raising the current result to the 10th power and multiplying in a to the power d, both reduced modulo 1337 to keep every value small. Repeating this once per digit correctly reconstructs a to the power b, one digit of the exponent at a time, without ever forming b as a whole number.

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: a is reduced modulo 1337 once, before the digit loop begins, so every multiplication inside the loop already works with a small base instead of repeatedly re-reducing a large one.
The inner loop computing the tenth power runs exactly 10 times, deliberately matching the identity's raise-to-the-10th-power step precisely, no more and no fewer.

The digit's own power is computed with its own small loop, running exactly digit times, since a single digit is always between 0 and 9, keeping that inner computation cheap regardless of how it is implemented.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(number of digits in b times 10), since each digit does up to 10 multiplications to compute the tenth power plus up to 9 more for the digit's own power.
Space: O(1) beyond the input digit array itself.
10. Further Optimization: Reusable Fast Power

Computing the tenth power with 10 sequential multiplications, and a digit's power with up to 9 more, works but repeats the same multiply-one-at-a-time pattern seen in the naive version of the Pow(x, n) problem. Replacing both of those steps with a proper fast modular exponentiation helper (the same exponentiation-by-squaring idea used there) reduces the operation count at each digit and produces cleaner, more reusable code.
Dry run for a = 2, b = [1, 0]

blocks.text: The same final result, 1024, is reached using a general purpose fast power function instead of a hardcoded loop of 10 multiplications.

blocks.caption: Further optimization: use a general fast power helper for both exponentiations at each digit

codes.python:
def mod_pow(base, exp, mod):
    base %= mod
    result = 1
    while exp > 0:
        if exp % 2 == 1:
            result = (result * base) % mod   # fold in this power of the base when the bit is set
        base = (base * base) % mod             # square the base for the next bit
        exp //= 2
    return result

def super_pow(a, b):
    a %= 1337
    result = 1
    for digit in b:                          # walk through b's digits, most significant first
        result = mod_pow(result, 10, 1337) * mod_pow(a, digit, 1337) % 1337  # combine via fast power
    return result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    a = 2
    b = [1, 0]
    print(super_pow(a, b))

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: modPow is written as a fully general helper, taking any base, exponent, and modulus, specifically so it can be reused for both the tenth-power step and the digit's-own-power step, rather than writing two separate specialized loops.

Inside modPow, base is squared and exp is halved every iteration, exactly the same exponentiation-by-squaring idea used in the standalone Pow(x, n) problem, just with a modulo reduction added after every multiplication.

Calling modPow(result, 10, 1337) and modPow(a, digit, 1337) separately, then multiplying their results together modulo 1337, mirrors the exact same two-piece combination the naive digit by digit version used, just computed more efficiently.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(number of digits in b times log 10), a modest but real reduction from the fixed 10 multiplications per digit, and a technique that scales even better if the base were larger than 10.
Space: O(1) beyond the input digit array.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

The core pattern here is processing a number that is too large to represent directly by working through its digits one at a time, combining an existing partial result with each new piece of information using a mathematical identity, exactly the same digit by digit spirit used in problems like Add Digits or Factorial Trailing Zeroes, applied here to modular exponentiation.
Common Mistakes

items: Attempting to reconstruct b as a single integer, which overflows or is outright impossible for the real constraint of up to 2000 digits.
Forgetting to reduce a modulo 1337 before starting, letting intermediate values grow unnecessarily large.
Mixing up the order of digits, b's array is given most significant digit first, which must be preserved when folding digits into the running result.

blocks.text: Interview Tips

This problem is a strong test of recognizing when a number is conceptually too large to handle directly and needs to be processed incrementally instead. Connecting the tenth-power identity back to modular exponentiation by squaring, the exact same technique from simpler power problems, shows the ability to compose known techniques to solve a much harder looking problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "b is too large to fit in an integer", think: process b one digit at a time using the tenth-power identity.
If the interviewer says "can you make the per-digit computation faster", think: replace the fixed 10-multiplication loop with a reusable modular exponentiation by squaring helper.
If the interviewer says "why take modulo 1337 so often", think: reducing after every multiplication is what keeps every intermediate value small, regardless of how many digits b has.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why can't b simply be parsed into a normal integer before computing the power?
Can you derive the identity a to the power (10x plus d) equals (a to the power x) to the 10th, times a to the power d, from first principles?
How would this approach change if the modulus were not a fixed constant like 1337, but a much larger prime?
Can you extend this digit by digit idea to bases other than 10, say processing b given in binary instead of decimal?
What is the overall time complexity in terms of the number of digits in b, and why does the fast power helper improve it?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Pow(x, n) and other fast exponentiation by squaring problems, whose modular exponentiation helper is reused directly here as the further optimization.
Add Digits and Factorial Trailing Zeroes, which share the same broader theme of processing a number through its digits or its prime factorization instead of its full literal value.

Any "the input is too large for a normal numeric type" problem, which generally requires processing the input as a string or digit array and combining pieces using a mathematical identity, exactly as done here.
Modular arithmetic problems in general, where reducing modulo a fixed value after every operation is what keeps a computation feasible despite astronomically large true intermediate values.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force approach is not just slow, it is impossible to run to completion for the real input constraints, since b itself may be unrepresentable. The digit by digit approach with naive tenth-power computation runs in O(digits of b) time with a small constant factor. Replacing that constant with a proper fast power helper trims the constant further and produces more reusable, general purpose code, both approaches use O(1) extra space beyond the input.
13. Final Summary

items: Pattern: processing a number too large to represent directly by working through its digits one at a time, combined with modular exponentiation by squaring.

Core Idea: a to the power (10 times x plus d) equals (a to the power x raised to the 10th power) times (a to the power d), letting the huge exponent b be folded in one digit at a time, with everything reduced modulo 1337 to stay small.
Time: infeasible in practice for the brute force, O(digits of b times 10) for the naive digit by digit version, O(digits of b times log 10) for the version using a reusable fast power helper.
Space: O(1) beyond the input digit array, across every feasible version.

Most Important Observation: an exponent too large to be a normal integer can still be processed correctly, one digit at a time, using the same shift-and-add logic that builds any multi-digit number, just applied to exponentiation instead of addition.

Interview Difficulty: the brute force is trivial to write but genuinely impossible to run; recognizing the digit by digit identity, and then reusing a proper fast power helper, is what demonstrates real command of modular exponentiation.
One line memory trick: raise the running result to the 10th, multiply in a to the new digit, all modulo 1337.
